turns.zh: 我们感谢您这样做，并且您可以为听众提供特别折扣。他们可以在vanta.com/lenny 上享受Vanta 优惠1,000 美元，即V-A-N-T-A.com/lenny，Vanta 优惠1,000 美元。谢谢你，克里斯蒂娜。

turns.speaker: Christina Cacioppo
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other big counterintuitive lessons from the journey that you think would be fun to share?
turns.zh: 您认为这段旅程中还有其他违反直觉的重大教训值得分享吗？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: One thing I really love about what we do in Monday is that we really love to take risks, not for the sake of it, but we are not afraid to do bold moves. And many times, when you want to do bold moves, you have a lot of concerns, especially when you start to be successful, because you are afraid that you are going to break everything that you built until now. And for me, one of the most pivotal moments in the company life is when we decided that, back in the days, as you said, we were a platform, but we had a go-to market of project management tool and we said, "Listen, people are doing so many different things on top of Monday. They are building a CRM of Monday and they are building a software for managing their dev cycles, and they are building so many different things," and we took a strategic decision to become a multi-product company which is built on top of this platform. And we actually did something which is really counterintuitive. (00:46:46): The first thought that comes to mind, at least for me, is, "Why maybe not just launch a new product, do it relatively on the side, gradually understand if it's successful? And if it would be successful, double click on it." But we actually did it in a very different way. We actually announced five different new products simultaneously on the same time, and we had so many... I can't stress enough how hard it is to think about it. Because I remember when we talked about and doing it, people say, "What? But we are going to confuse our current users and it's going to have conversion. And how are we going to do the marketing now when we have so many different go-to markets? And the sales, they don't know how to navigate people to different... And what about pricing?" So many different concerns, but we decided to do it because we really want to create a pivotal leap. (00:47:46): And I think that, in that sense, fast-forward to this day, part of these products were really successful. For instance, Monday sale CRM is going faster than Monday back in the days, when it's amazing to see it, and-
turns.zh: 我真正喜欢我们周一所做的一件事是，我们真的喜欢冒险，不是为了冒险，但我们不害怕采取大胆的行动。很多时候，当你想做大胆的举动时，你会有很多担忧，尤其是当你开始成功时，因为你担心你会破坏你迄今为止建立的一切。对我来说，公司生活中最关键的时刻之一是当我们决定，正如你所说，我们是一个平台，但我们有一个项目管理工具的市场，我们说，“听着，人们在周一做很多不同的事情。他们正在构建周一的 CRM，他们正在构建一个用于管理他们的开发周期的软件，他们正在构建很多不同的东西，”我们做出了一个战略决策，成为一家建立在这个平台。我们实际上做了一些非常违反直觉的事情。 (00:46:46)：至少对我来说，首先想到的是，“为什么不直接推出一个新产品，相对地做一下，逐渐了解它是否成功？如果成功，双击它。”但我们实际上以一种非常不同的方式做到了。实际上，我们在同一时间同时发布了五种不同的新产品，而且我们有这么多......我无法强调这是多么难以想象。因为我记得当我们谈论和做这件事时，人们说，“什么？但是我们会让我们当前的用户感到困惑，这将会带来转化。当我们有这么多不同的目标市场时，我们现在要如何进行营销？而销售，他们不知道如何引导人们走向不同的……那么定价又如何呢？”有很多不同的担忧，但我们决定这样做，因为我们真的想创造一个关键的飞跃。 (00:47:46)：我认为，从这个意义上说，快进到今天，这些产品的一部分确实取得了成功。例如，周一销售 CRM 的速度比过去的周一要快，当时看到它真是令人惊奇，而且 -

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: In the days when it's amazing to see it. And some of them we understood that they don't need to be separate products and we collapse them back to the main product. But the point is, is that we managed to learn and to change both internally at the company, how the perception of everyone around what we are building, but also externally. (00:48:21): This move changed dramatically the competitive landscape that we live in. And, I think there was a lot of friction. Many people at the company were having a lot of friction with it. It was really, really hard. (00:48:35): But looking back it's such, I'm so happy with this move and the fact that we did it like that because just imagine what would happen if we would choose one of them and it wasn't the successful products. And our conclusion can be that multi product won't work for us. (00:48:52): We really managed to transform the company in a very short amount of time and also to create new reality. And I think that people need to remember that and I'm constantly reminding it to myself. And I think this is something that we are constantly working with each other in order to make sure that we remember that not taking bold risks, not making bold moves, it's a risk for itself. Okay? (00:49:21): And many times people want the inertia, people want just the incremental value. But if you want to do leaps many times you need to let go of things that were successful for you in the past. And this is very counterintuitive and we did a lot of mental models to help us cope with it. (00:49:38): So I remember that when we were small and we had for instance 20,000 paying customers, so we said, "Listen, but most of Monday's customers are not customers of Monday, yet. So we need to think about them, as well." (00:49:51): And this is something that really helps you because many times you need to do things that affect the current success that you have. But I think this is another very, very important thing that I am constantly reminding to myself.
turns.zh: 在看到它令人惊奇的日子里。其中一些我们知道它们不需要是单独的产品，我们将它们折叠回主要产品。但关键是，我们成功地学习并改变了公司内部以及外部每个人对我们正在建设的产品的看法。 (00:48:21)：这一举措极大地改变了我们生活的竞争格局。而且，我认为存在很多摩擦。公司里的很多人都对此产生了很多摩擦。这真的非常非常难。 (00:48:35)：但回想起来，我对这一举措以及我们这样做的事实感到非常满意，因为想象一下，如果我们选择其中一个而不是成功的产品，会发生什么。我们的结论是，多种产品对我们不起作用。 (00:48:52)：我们确实在很短的时间内成功地实现了公司转型，并创造了新的现实。我认为人们需要记住这一点，我也不断提醒自己。我认为这是我们不断相互合作的事情，以确保我们记住，不冒大胆的风险，不采取大胆的行动，这本身就是一种风险。好的？ (00:49:21)：很多时候人们想要的是惯性，人们想要的只是增量价值。但如果你想多次实现跨越，你就需要放弃过去对你来说成功的事情。这是非常违反直觉的，我们做了很多心理模型来帮助我们应对它。 (00:49:38)：所以我记得当我们规模较小时，我们有 20,000 名付费客户，所以我们说，“听着，但大多数周一的客户还不是周一的客户。所以我们也需要考虑他们。” (00:49:51)：这确实对您有帮助，因为很多时候您需要做一些影响当前成功的事情。但我认为这是我不断提醒自己的另一件非常非常重要的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's kind of this other recurring theme that I'm noticing of just thinking big and taking leaps. And I love this point you made of not doing that is actually a big risk. Not taking a risk is a big risk. That's a really powerful point. (00:50:20): And it's innately scary to do something risky. And so, I love the push here of just take more risks because it's so easy. And this comes back again to the beginning of the conversation where we're just building things the way they've always been built. And looking back and what have we even done? What have we done over this year of hard work and tons of features? (00:50:39): I think a lot of companies get in that place where they're just like, "What are we?" Like in our B and B, I had this exact, Brian is constant like, "What are we even shipping all these billions of experiments that are moving the numbers? What are we even doing? I don't know anything that we ship that's really exciting." (00:50:52): And so, I think this is a really good reminder and push to just think bigger and you need to take big leaps. So, love that. Is there any other big counterintuitive lessons before we move in a different direction?
turns.zh: 我注意到还有一个反复出现的主题，那就是大胆思考并取得飞跃。我喜欢你所说的这一点，不这样做实际上是一个很大的风险。不冒险就是一个很大的风险。这是一个非常有力的观点。 (00:50:20)：做冒险的事情本质上是令人恐惧的。因此，我喜欢这里提倡承担更多风险，因为这很容易。这又回到了谈话的开始，我们只是按照一贯的方式来构建事物。回顾过去，我们到底做了什么？经过这一年的努力和大量的功能，我们做了什么？ (00:50:39)：我认为很多公司都会陷入这样的境地：“我们是什么？”就像在我们的 B 和 B 中一样，我有这样的说法，Brian 总是这样说：“我们究竟在运送这些数十亿个改变数字的实验？我们到底在做什么？我不知道我们运送的任何东西是真正令人兴奋的。” (00:50:52)：所以，我认为这是一个非常好的提醒，并推动你想得更大，你需要迈出一大步。所以，喜欢那个。在我们转向不同的方向之前，还有其他重大的违反直觉的教训吗？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I really believe that many time, like spending more time on working on something will not yield to better results or to better products. And I think that many times we, as people, that are building products for others get to a point where the feedback that we want to get in the bottom of our heart is like, " Wow, what an amazing product you have built." (00:51:33): And I think this is a very bad feedback to get for initial things that you are doing. Because it means that, I feel that in many ways, the point in which you make real people use your product is really scary. Because you suddenly put your work out there and then in order to actually, and you are afraid that they will say, "Listen, it's a lousy product, it's not a good product." But actually we really encourage people to get really fast production, to put traps for themselves that is called by time and not by effort. (00:52:12): And, many times I saw that more time creates more questions. It creates more complications. It creates more assumptions that we put for ourselves in thinking what our users need. And we invent things. (00:52:29): And we do it all from good reasons. We want people to like what we build, we want them to get value. But, for me, this is a very important point that many times using, like the setting traps mechanism of saying, "Listen, we have three weeks, let's think about it." (00:52:50): And [inaudible 00:52:51] by time, it makes you extremely focused. And this is very important because we really want to get feedback from customers that say, "Yeah, listen, this is on the direction. I'm still missing this and this and this. And also we really love the fact of this is not a good product." (00:53:11): And I can give you a recent example. Even when now we work with big customers and, of course, there are different ways to implement what I said than you are a small startup. But we are building a new offering of enterprise work management. Think about it like a way of managing projects. It's a huge, huge scale. Thousands of projects like tens of thousands of employees and so on. (00:53:33): So, I really love using the deadline trap and it makes you focused, it makes you sharper in thinking. And, we just had a recent example with the offering I was telling you about of enterprise work management, managing project at scale. And this is an enterprise product. (00:53:48): So you have all the reasons in the world to say, "No, I can't release it, yet. I need more time. I need to do more things. They won't use it. They need this and this and this." (00:53:58): And I think that we actually released the first alpha version to them. And we got a feedback of, "Listen guys, this is premature. We need more comprehensive value." But we got exactly the feedback of what, and this is priceless. (00:54:13): And my response to the teams is, "Well done. I think you did an amazing job in releasing it and making sure." Because many times, being so afraid of releasing it and thinking, "If I just have 1, 2, 3 more weeks, I will build a better product." I think it's not true.
turns.zh: 我真的相信很多时候，比如花更多的时间在某件事上，不会产生更好的结果或更好的产品。我认为，很多时候，我们作为人，在为他人构建产品时，都会达到这样的程度：我们希望在内心深处得到的反馈是这样的：“哇，你构建了多么令人惊叹的产品。” (00:51:33)：我认为对于你最初所做的事情来说，这是一个非常糟糕的反馈。因为这意味着，我觉得从很多方面来说，让真正的人使用你的产品这一点真的很可怕。因为你突然把你的工作放在那里，然后为了实际上，你担心他们会说，“听着，这是一个糟糕的产品，它不是一个好产品。”但实际上我们真的鼓励人们获得非常快的生产，为自己设置陷阱，这是时间而不是努力的结果。 (00:52:12)：而且，很多时候我发现更多的时间会产生更多的问题。它会造成更多的并发症。它为我们在思考用户需求时做出了更多假设。我们发明了东西。 (00:52:29)：我们这样做都是有充分理由的。我们希望人们喜欢我们构建的东西，我们希望他们获得价值。但是，对我来说，这是非常重要的一点，很多时候都会使用，就像设置陷阱机制一样，“听着，我们有三个星期的时间，让我们考虑一下。” (00:52:50)：[听不清 00:52:51] 随着时间的推移，它会让你非常专注。这非常重要，因为我们真的希望得到客户的反馈，“是的，听着，这是方向。我仍然想念这个、这个和这个。而且我们真的很喜欢这个事实，因为这不是一个好产品。” (00:53:11)：我可以给你举一个最近的例子。即使现在我们与大客户合作，当然，与小型初创公司相比，实施我所说的方法也有不同的方法。但我们正在构建一种新的企业工作管理产品。将其视为一种管理项目的方式。这是一个巨大、巨大的规模。数千个项目，例如数万名员工等等。 (00:53:33)：所以，我真的很喜欢使用截止日期陷阱，它让你集中注意力，让你的思维更加敏锐。而且，我们刚刚有一个最近的例子，其中包含我向您介绍的企业工作管理、大规模管理项目的产品。这是一个企业产品。 (00:53:48)：所以你有充分的理由说：“不，我还不能发布它。我需要更多时间。我需要做更多事情。他们不会使用它。他们需要这个、这个、这个。” (00:53:58)：我认为我们实际上向他们发布了第一个 alpha 版本。我们得到的反馈是：“听着，伙计们，这还为时过早。我们需要更全面的价值。”但我们得到了确切的反馈，这是无价的。 (00:54:13)：我对团队的回应是：“干得好。我认为你们在发布和确保方面做得非常出色。”因为很多时候，我非常害怕发布它，并想：“如果我再多 1、2、3 周的时间，我就能打造出更好的产品。”我认为这不是真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such good advice. It resonates so much with recent other conversations I've had. So, just to clarify what you're saying, basically, you have a time box. (00:54:42): When you say traps, it's basically a set amount of time. We're going to spend three weeks on this feature and if we don't hit the three weeks, we just cut scope, essentially. Is that the idea?
turns.zh: 这是很好的建议。它与我最近进行的其他对话产生了很大的共鸣。所以，为了澄清你所说的，基本上，你有一个时间框。 (00:54:42)：当你说陷阱时，它基本上是指一段固定的时间。我们将花三周的时间来开发这个功能，如果我们没有达到三周的时间，我们基本上就会缩小范围。是这个想法吗？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I think, yeah, it's like this is the basic version of it.
turns.zh: 我想，是的，这就是它的基本版本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: But now, for us, we really want and we really love doing it as an exercise for ourself. For instance, let's say, now as a public company we say, "Listen, we're working on something. We want to announce it on the next earning. And put a trap for ourselves." (00:55:09): Why? Because, again, it makes you sharp. It makes you super focused about things. And I think that in many ways this results in a much better product because you are not building things that you invented. You are staying really true to what your users needs, the real core of the value. (00:55:32): And, it's really funny to see the dynamics of teams when they are planning from the bottom up. So, it starts with something that like let's say you've done everything great. Okay, you have the opportunity, you understand, you have the KPIs, everything is in place, but now you're starting to plan it. (00:55:50): And, suddenly, people are raising concerns and issues. And it becomes a sport to say what can go wrong and like being fear- driven. And then you tend to protect yourself and adding more content and more content. And then when you see what happens, it's actually, it's going to be shipped in two years. (00:56:11): And then we say, "Okay, no. Okay, we have earnings in two months. What can we ship to this earnings? And let's put a tab." And then you suddenly see the conversation changes. First of all, it makes everyone really focused on what's the core of the value. And it removes all the theoretical discussions that people have and things like that. (00:56:31): And, the results are amazing. And you need to remember when you do it, you need to continue afterwards like according to feedbacks and not let it go just but what you did in the first version. But, in many ways, I really love the fact that the first version get the feedback, which is not everything is perfect because if this is the feedback, it means that we built too much and probably it's not focused product enough. (00:56:58): And when you build a lot of features, this can be like a death by a thousand cuts because in each corner of the product you add more than you need.
turns.zh: 但现在，对于我们来说，我们真的想要并且我们真的很喜欢将其作为对自己的锻炼。举例来说，现在作为一家上市公司，我们说：“听着，我们正在做某件事。我们想在下一次财报中宣布它。并为自己设置一个陷阱。” (00:55:09)：为什么？因为，它再次让你变得敏锐。它让你超级专注于事情。我认为，从很多方面来说，这会带来更好的产品，因为你并不是在建造自己发明的东西。您真正忠于用户的需求，即价值的真正核心。 (00:55:32)：而且，看到团队自下而上规划时的动态真的很有趣。所以，一切都是从这样的事情开始的：假设你已经把一切都做得很好了。好吧，你有机会，你明白，你有 KPI，一切都已就位，但现在你开始计划了。 (00:55:50)：突然之间，人们提出了担忧和问题。说出可能出问题的地方已经成为一种运动，就像被恐惧驱使一样。然后你就会倾向于保护自己并添加更多的内容。然后当你看到发生的事情时，实际上，它将在两年内发货。 (00:56:11)：然后我们说，“好吧，不。好吧，我们在两个月内就有了收入。我们可以为此收入寄送什么？让我们记下标签。”然后你突然发现对话发生了变化。首先，它让每个人真正关注价值的核心是什么。它消除了人们进行的所有理论讨论以及类似的事情。 (00:56:31)：而且，结果是惊人的。而且你需要记住，当你这样做时，你需要像根据反馈一样继续之后，而不是仅仅放弃你在第一个版本中所做的事情。但是，从很多方面来说，我真的很喜欢第一个版本得到的反馈，这并不是一切都是完美的，因为如果这是反馈，则意味着我们构建了太多，并且可能不够专注于产品。 (00:56:58)：当您构建大量功能时，这可能就像千刀万剐，因为您在产品的每个角落添加的内容都超出了您的需要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's so much here that connects the other conversation we just had. We had Gaurav Misra, he's the CEO of Captions and he made this point that if people aren't complaining about your product, you want to see people complaining because that means they care. There's something there that they care about. If you're not hearing any complaints, they could care less about what you're building and that's a bad sign.
turns.zh: 是的，这里有很多东西可以连接我们刚刚进行的其他谈话。我们有 Gaurav Misra，他是 Captions 的首席执行官，他指出，如果人们没有抱怨你的产品，你希望看到人们抱怨，因为这意味着他们关心。那里有他们关心的东西。如果您没有听到任何投诉，他们可能不太关心您正在构建的内容，这是一个坏兆头。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I really loved it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢它。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Their company actually goes to the extreme of what you're describing. Every engineer ships a marketable feature every week. That's their pace.
turns.zh: 他们的公司实际上已经达到了你所描述的极端。每个工程师每周都会发布一个适销对路的功能。这就是他们的节奏。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I really connected to it. And by the way, about user feedback, I think it's really nice because many times people associate, like they only measure themselves by user feedback and a specific point. And I think this is also maybe something that is counterintuitive. Not every customer feedback is the feedback that will drive you to the end result of the best product out there. (00:58:06): There are many aspects to it. I can share just one example about us. We, as a, in the beginning of the company, we, for instance, didn't want to have a free trial. And part of it is that we really wanted to hear feedback about our product only from people that the product means something to them. The best proxy for that is that they are paying because it means they get real value. And you know, in that sense it helped us at the beginning to stay super focused about separating the wheat from the shaft with the customer's feedback. So I think it's a super important point and we need to take customer feedback in context.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢它。顺便说一句，关于用户反馈，我认为这真的很好，因为很多时候人们会联想到，就像他们只通过用户反馈和特定点来衡量自己一样。我认为这也许也是违反直觉的。并非所有客户反馈都会促使您获得最佳产品的最终结果。 (00:58:06)：它有很多方面。我只能分享一个关于我们的例子。例如，作为公司成立之初，我们不想进行免费试用。部分原因是我们真的只想听到人们对我们产品的反馈，认为该产品对他们有意义。最好的体现是他们付费，因为这意味着他们获得了真正的价值。你知道，从这个意义上说，它帮助我们一开始就根据客户的反馈集中精力将小麦与轴分离。所以我认为这是非常重要的一点，我们需要结合实际情况考虑客户的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other really interesting point here that you're making is this idea of, we had, I think I mentioned this already, Ryan Singer, he's the creator of this method, Shape Up, which is very centered around appetites over deadlines. (00:59:02): There's so many, everyone listening to this has probably gone through an exercise where like, "Let's redo our landing page." And it's like, "Yeah, it'll probably have some impact. Let's spend some time on this." (00:59:11): It ends up taking six months. And everyone's like, "Why did we spend six months redoing this freaking landing page? I would've given it three weeks and then moved on." (00:59:21): And the way to do that is you just commit upfront, "We will spend three weeks on this. We'll get as much done as we can in three weeks and then we'll move on." (00:59:29): People talk about this very hard to actually do so I love that's how you actually approach some of these bigger features you work on. Do you guys practice Shape Up by any chance or this is just a thing you do?
turns.zh: 你在这里提出的另一个非常有趣的观点是，我们有，我想我已经提到过这一点，瑞安·辛格（Ryan Singer），他是这种方法“Shape Up”的创造者，该方法非常以截止日期前的欲望为中心。 (00:59:02)：有很多，每个听这个的人可能都经历过类似的练习，“让我们重做我们的登陆页面。”就像，“是的，它可能会产生一些影响。让我们花一些时间在这上面。” (00:59:11)：最终花了六个月的时间。每个人都会说，“为什么我们要花六个月的时间重做这个该死的登陆页面？我本来会花三周的时间，然后继续前进。” (00:59:21)：要做到这一点，你只需预先承诺，“我们将花三周的时间来做这件事。我们将在三周内完成尽可能多的工作，然后继续前进。” (00:59:29)：人们谈论这一点很难真正做到，所以我喜欢这就是你实际处理你正在开发的一些更大功能的方式。你们是偶然练习Shape Up 还是这只是你们所做的事情？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: No, actually, I wasn't that familiar with it, but I definitely going to check it out. Yeah.
turns.zh: 不，实际上，我不太熟悉它，但我肯定会去看看。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Yeah, it's a whole method. And I think the episode right before this is actually that episode. Okay. Let me go in a different direction and kind of keep extracting lessons from this journey because that was a really fruitful place to go. (00:59:54): So let me ask you this question. What's one thing that you wish you'd known before stepping into the role that you're in today?
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。是的，这是一个完整的方法。我认为之前的那一集实际上就是那一集。好的。让我朝不同的方向前进，并不断从这次旅程中汲取教训，因为那是一个非常富有成效的地方。 (00:59:54)：所以让我问你这个问题。在担任今天的职位之前，您希望自己知道的一件事是什么？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: This is an interesting question. I think there are many aspects to it and maybe if I'll take the personal aspects. So I've been in charge of the product and technology from since I joined the company. But with that, my role has changed, I think, dozens of times. (01:00:21): I feel I'm very fortunate to work in one company but actually work in dozens of different companies. Think about the scale that we talked about. Each point is a different, it's actually a different company and a different role and a different challenge. (01:00:36): And I think that something that maybe is counterintuitive personally, for me, was that in many of the phases that we undergrowed with, I felt that what got me to this phase is not necessarily what's going to make me successful in the next phase. (01:00:55): And if I want to be even more blunt, there will personally times when suddenly I saw how my biggest strength, for instance like, mastering all the details and having everything in my head knowing exactly what's happening on every corner of what we do. This was probably something that gave a lot of value when we were small. (01:01:22): But, as we got bigger, I think it suddenly created even the damage continuing to do the same thing. And in many ways, it takes time to do this realization. And I think that a good advice that I would love to have is that don't be afraid again to let go of things that you think are superpowers. (01:01:47): Many times your superpowers that brought you to this point and made you successful, many times you think that if you let it go you won't be successful and it's frightening. But, I really feel that you need to constantly evaluate what your current role is actually, is actually what is the role? And what is needed in order to be successful in it and not continue with the inertia? (01:02:12): And this is something that I wish someone has told me. Yeah. It took me time in many cases, you know? Many cases I did it too late.
turns.zh: 这是一个有趣的问题。我认为这有很多方面，也许我会考虑个人方面。所以从我加入公司开始，我就一直负责产品和技术。但随之而来的是，我认为我的角色已经改变了数十次。 (01:00:21)：我觉得我很幸运能够在一家公司工作，但实际上我在数十家不同的公司工作。想想我们谈到的规模。每个点都是不同的，实际上是不同的公司、不同的角色和不同的挑战。 (01:00:36)：我认为对我个人而言，可能违反直觉的是，在我们成长不足的许多阶段中，我觉得让我进入这个阶段的东西不一定会让我在下一阶段取得成功。 (01:00:55)：如果我想更直白的话，我个人有时会突然看到自己最大的优势，例如，掌握所有细节，让一切都在我的脑海中，准确地知道我们所做的每个角落正在发生的事情。这可能是我们小时候很有价值的东西。 (01:01:22)：但是，随着我们变得更大，我认为它突然造成了持续做同样事情的损害。从很多方面来说，实现这一目标需要时间。我认为我希望得到的一个好建议是，不要再次害怕放弃你认为是超能力的东西。 (01:01:47): 很多时候你的超能力让你走到了这一步并让你成功，很多时候你认为如果你放手你就不会成功，这很可怕。但是，我真的觉得你需要不断地评估你现在的角色到底是什么，到底是什么角色？为了取得成功而不是继续惯性，需要什么？ (01:02:12)：我希望有人告诉我这一点。是的。很多时候我花了很多时间，你知道吗？很多时候我做得太晚了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that helped you realize this or get good at this? Is it like coaching? Is it just doing it and surviving and failing and be like, "Oh, I see."
turns.zh: 有什么事情可以帮助您认识到这一点或擅长这一点吗？是不是像教练一样？难道只是做事然后生存然后失败然后说“哦，我明白了”。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I think all of the above. I think that one sign for that, for me, was that in many cases I felt I'm doing a very good job. But then people, it can be like, I'll give you an example. Okay? (01:02:50): For instance, doing a company like Leadership QBRs. Okay, quarterly business reviews. So, when we just started it with it very early, I would actually tell about everything. (01:03:04): And I remember one meeting that I went out of the meeting and I say, "Wow, I really managed to convey everything and explain everything in a very articulated way." (01:03:16): And one of my colleagues in the core leadership team said, "Well, I didn't understand anything. What is the bottom line of all of this?" And it was like you suddenly realize that what you thought is good is not necessarily what the other people needs from you at this point. (01:03:43): And after understanding that, I went and ask, "What would be beneficial for you?" He said, "Listen, I want to keep in my head the three most meaningful things that you are currently facing with. I don't want to hear everything." (01:03:55): And it's hard. But, this was the point for me that I realized that I need to change. And I need to change something and the requirements are different. (01:04:10): At the beginning I tried to say, "But, listen, it's important that you know you are sticking to it." Right? But we need to let it go sometimes and think from the beginning.
turns.zh: 我认为以上都是。我认为对我来说，一个迹象是，在很多情况下我觉得自己做得很好。但人们可能会说，我给你们举个例子。好的？ (01:02:50)：例如，做一家像领导力 QBR 这样的公司。好的，季度业务回顾。所以，当我们很早就开始的时候，我实际上会告诉一切。 (01:03:04)：我记得有一次会议结束后我说：“哇，我真的成功地以非常清晰的方式传达了所有内容并解释了所有内容。” (01:03:16)：我的一位核心领导团队同事说：“好吧，我什么都不懂。这一切的底线是什么？”就像你突然意识到，你认为好的东西不一定是其他人此时需要你提供的东西。 (01:03:43)：明白这一点后，我去问：“什么对你有好处？”他说：“听着，我想把你目前面临的三件最有意义的事情记在脑子里。我不想听到所有的事情。” (01:03:55)：这很难。但是，这对我来说是我意识到我需要改变的一点。我需要改变一些东西并且要求不同。 (01:04:10)：一开始我试图说，“但是，听着，重要的是你知道自己正在坚持下去。”正确的？但有时我们需要放手，从头开始思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this phrase that someone shared on this podcast once where, as you rise in your career, you often go from the person that is pitching leaders on something to the person being pitched. And that's a really weird place to move from, having to learn how to give great feedback, delegate, let go of things. And I love that this is a good example of that. (01:04:44): Since we're getting a little vulnerable and open about stuff, I want to try this question. You've done a lot of podcasts, you've done a lot of interviews, you've been all over the place. Is there anything you haven't shared anywhere else that might be helpful to share here about the journey you've been on?
turns.zh: 有人在这个播客上分享过这样一句话，当你在职业生涯中崛起时，你经常会从向领导者推销某件事的人变成被推销的人。这是一个非常奇怪的地方，必须学习如何提供良好的反馈、委派、放手。我喜欢这是一个很好的例子。 (01:04:44)：由于我们变得有点脆弱和开放，我想尝试这个问题。你做过很多播客，做过很多采访，去过很多地方。对于您所经历的旅程，是否有任何您未在其他地方分享过的内容可能对在这里分享有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Yeah, so, maybe continuing with the same point. It's a crazy journey and it's a crazy personal journey. If you think about it, I remember Roy once said, "If someone would've interviewed me to a public company of, like I would say $10 billion in market cap and managing 2,500 employees, I'm not sure that I would interview myself and get myself to the job." (01:05:27): And, for me, there were a lot of moments and it's constantly happening. You know, when things are going sideways and things doesn't work, and you see so many things are breaking down. You can be on the same day super happy and suddenly on the lowest point there is. (01:05:49): And I can show you, no. Many times I've asked myself whether I'm the right person to lead it, whether we need someone that is coming with all the experience to this phase. And I remember talked to that day with Ron. He tell me, he told me something, "Listen, first of all, as the one who built it, no one would be able to do it like you." (01:06:14): And I think it's an important thing to remember when times are tough. I really believe that if you have the passion, and if you have the will, and if you are willing to do the hard work in order to constantly adjust and evolve and to be vulnerable and also to say about yourself, "I didn't understand something. Now, I need to learn it and I need to deal things differently." (01:06:44): It's a very important point if you want to do this kind of a journey. And it's hard. And something I can share, I can reassure everyone that are listening to us, if you are feeling it, you are not the only one. Everyone are feeling it from once in a while. Be confident about yourself. Be vulnerable in order to learn and to evolve. (01:07:06): And I really love to do a mental exercise of saying, like we said about the product. So, let's say I'm Daniel of next six months. How do I want to look back on these six months? And what do I want to say about myself that I learned that I evolved? And this helped you get out from the state of everything is okay, I am good. And it makes you want to learn and want to evolve. (01:07:37): And also staying doing mode. I don't believe in, I think one thing that really characterized me is that it can be very difficult and very challenging time. But on the next day, I'm already bouncing back with energy. And in order to come and do things and win it. (01:08:04): And there are a lot of things that we, as leaders, needs to do in order to help ourselves to keep this mental state. So, I like to run. I like to do things that are unrelated to work in order to get back to my center. (01:08:21): But then quickly bounce back and to really believe in myself, in the team around me. So this, yeah, this is something maybe very personal, but I am pretty sure I'm not the only one feeling it.
turns.zh: 是的，所以，也许继续同样的观点。这是一次疯狂的旅程，也是一次疯狂的个人旅程。如果你仔细想想，我记得罗伊曾经说过，“如果有人来面试我一家市值 100 亿美元、管理着 2,500 名员工的上市公司，我不确定我是否会面试自己并获得这份工作。” (01:05:27)：对我来说，有很多时刻，而且它不断发生。你知道，当事情出现问题并且事情不起作用时，你会看到很多事情都崩溃了。你可能会在同一天超级快乐，但突然就跌入最低点。 (01:05:49)：我可以告诉你，不。我多次问自己，我是否是领导这个阶段的合适人选，我们是否需要一个拥有这一阶段所有经验的人。我记得那天和罗恩谈过。他告诉我，他告诉我一些事情，“听着，首先，作为建造它的人，没有人能够像你一样做到这一点。” (01:06:14)：我认为在困难时期记住这一点很重要。我真的相信，如果你有激情，如果你有意愿，如果你愿意努力工作，以便不断调整和发展，并保持脆弱，并且对自己说，“我不明白一些事情。现在，我需要学习它，我需要以不同的方式处理事情。” (01:06:44)：如果你想做这样的旅程，这是非常重要的一点。这很难。我可以分享一些东西，我可以向每个正在听我们讲话的人保证，如果你有这种感觉，你并不是唯一一个。每个人都会时不时地感受到这一点。对自己要有信心。为了学习和发展，要变得脆弱。 (01:07:06)：我真的很喜欢做一个心理练习，就像我们对产品所说的那样。那么，假设我是未来六个月的丹尼尔。我想如何回顾这六个月？当我了解到自己是进化的时候，我想对自己说什么？这帮助你摆脱了“一切都好，我很好”的状态。它让你想要学习并想要发展。 (01:07:37)：并且还保持做事模式。我不相信，我认为真正让我有特点的一件事是，这可能是非常困难和充满挑战的时期。但第二天，我已经恢复了精力。为了来做事并赢得胜利。 (01:08:04)：作为领导者，我们需要做很多事情来帮助自己保持这种精神状态。所以，我喜欢跑步。我喜欢做一些与工作无关的事情，以便回到我的中心。 (01:08:21)：但很快就会恢复过来，真正相信自己，相信我周围的团队。所以，是的，这可能是非常个人化的事情，但我很确定我不是唯一有这种感觉的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate you sharing that. There's a post that I did a long time ago with a coach and it was about imposter syndrome. And she made this really powerful point that you are actually an imposter in the role you're in. You've never done this before. (01:08:54): Most people are imposters in their role. They've never been a chief product officer. In a lot of cases they've never led teams this large. And first of all just realize that you actually are. (01:09:05): And second of all, that's okay and most people are like you said. And then third of all, this advice you shared about how to work through that is really powerful. Just like know many people feel this way. (01:09:15): Work hard, I think, is a really important part of this. Just like know there's another day and that you can bounce back.
turns.zh: 我很感激你分享这一点。很久以前我和一位教练一起发表了一篇关于冒名顶替综合症的文章。她提出了一个非常有力的观点，即你实际上是你所扮演的角色的冒名顶替者。你以前从未这样做过。 (01:08:54)：大多数人在他们的角色中都是冒名顶替者。他们从来没有担任过首席产品官。在很多情况下，他们从来没有领导过这么大的团队。首先要意识到你确实是这样。 (01:09:05)：其次，这没关系，大多数人都像你说的那样。第三，您分享的关于如何解决这个问题的建议非常有效。就像知道很多人都有这种感觉一样。 (01:09:15)：我认为，努力工作是其中非常重要的一部分。就像知道还有另一天，你可以反弹一样。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Remember that everyone are people. No one is born to be in the world that he's currently at. And another thing that in Monday we're scaling so fast. So even people that are coming with experience and I had the chance to see it over and over again, because we're going so fast, each one of us will get to a point, which is the first time he's doing it sooner or later. (01:09:47): So, experience matters and we have a lot of people that are coming and bringing experience from the outside. But also remember that and remember that everyone are people and no one was born in a position.
turns.zh: 请记住，每个人都是人。没有人天生就生活在他现在所处的世界里。周一我们的另一件事是扩张速度如此之快。因此，即使是那些有经验的人，我也有机会一遍又一遍地看到它，因为我们进展得太快，我们每个人迟早都会到达一个点，这是他第一次这样做。 (01:09:47)：所以，经验很重要，我们有很多人从外部带来经验。但也要记住这一点，记住每个人都是人，没有人出生在一个职位上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And in companies like yours, people have described it as every six months you have a new job.
turns.zh: 是的。在像你们这样的公司中，人们将其描述为每六个月就有一份新工作。

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Exactly. Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cheryl Sandberg once did a talk that I was at where people are complaining. It was just like, "So much is changing, we're growing. The culture is not as strong as it was, and there's just like things not working. Our processes are no, hiring is hard." (01:10:26): And she's just like, "This is the problems you want because you're growing very fast and that's very good. Versus, if you were not growing, it'd be much more painful and hard. So, be thankful this is the problems you're facing."
turns.zh: 谢丽尔·桑德伯格（Cheryl Sandberg）曾经做过一次演讲，说我就在人们抱怨的地方。就像是，“发生了很多变化，我们正在成长。文化不像以前那么强大，而且有些事情不起作用。我们的流程不行，招聘很困难。” (01:10:26)：她就说，“这就是你想要的问题，因为你成长得非常快，这很好。相反，如果你没有成长，那就会更加痛苦和困难。所以，要庆幸这就是你面临的问题。”

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: I couldn't agree more.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about things breaking along the way and things you had to deal with. Is there an example of something? I love these stories of just maybe a moment of crisis along the journey where you thought like, "Okay, things are going to fall apart. This is over. See you, everyone."
turns.zh: 你们谈到了一路上发生的事情以及必须处理的事情。有什么例子吗？我喜欢这些故事，讲述旅途中可能出现的危机时刻，你会想，“好吧，事情要崩溃了。一切都结束了。再见，大家。”

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Yeah. To be honest, we have so many. But, again, this is the problems that you are lucky to have. But, yeah, maybe I'll give you an example. (01:11:08): I remember this day that someone from our customer success team has approached me and say, "Listen, Daniel, we have a spike in performance issues in the board." And again, our boards is this table of think about it like of data. (01:11:25): And on each time we add new functionality and we make the platform more mature, people are taking it to the extreme. So, if you look back eight years ago, so this kind of tables usually had like, let's say, five columns and 100 rows. And if you look about it today, it's like hundreds of columns, tens of thousands of rows. (01:11:45): And so, performance is always a challenge and struggle in making sure that everything works smoothly. And this is also a value to us. We really believe that performance is the number one feature that makes people use your system. So, we came to me-
turns.zh: 是的。说实话，我们有很多。但是，这又是你幸运地遇到的问题。但是，是的，也许我会给你举个例子。 (01:11:08)：我记得今天，我们客户成功团队的一个人找到我说：“听着，丹尼尔，我们董事会的绩效问题激增。”再说一次，我们的董事会就是这张像数据一样思考的表格。 (01:11:25)：每次我们添加新功能并使平台变得更加成熟时，人们都会将其发挥到极致。所以，如果你回顾八年前，这种表通常有 5 列和 100 行。如果你今天看一下，它就像数百列，数万行。 (01:11:45)：因此，为了确保一切顺利进行，性能始终是一项挑战和斗争。这对我们来说也是一种价值。我们坚信性能是人们使用您的系统的首要特征。所以，我们来找我——

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: System. He came to me, and I remember that suddenly seeing the spike in the tickets, it's super hard, right? You say, wow, it's something super hard. You don't necessarily have a magic wand of fixing it immediately. And what we did, we actually, again, connected everyone to it. The first thing they did was taking disc golf to everyone in the team and showing and thinking together what we can do. And we did a lot of things and we worked really hard and we managed to make this situation better. And then time passed by and you are continuing, and then it happened again. And I can share that on the third time I said, "Okay, we had enough. We need to think totally different in a different way." And back in the days, this is where I think many of our core long-term projects have born. The signature one would be MondayDB. It's a name we use for an underlying data infrastructure that we've been building in the last three years or so. (01:13:19): Think about a very small team and a very small startup. I remember the day that we said, listen, we need few of our most talented people that are now not going to contribute features anymore. We are putting them on a separate place, and let's think and solve this problem while thinking about 100X. And it really, in many ways, so different from what we talked about in so many other of the examples, right? And I think now we said, listen, instead of being fixing an issue, we want this to be our competitive edge. We have a very unique product architecture where everyone can build their own schemas of the table. And it's a crazy thing in terms of technology behind it. We want to do something that will not only solve the problem, but also will serve us as a competitive edge. And we took a huge risk because we took a lot of people and put them aside for that, or not a lot of people, but the very talented people. (01:14:27): And I think in retrospect, by the way we released MondayDB, I think one and a half years ago, the first version, it did a huge, huge change for customers. And in many ways, this is what actually makes us today a platform which is enterprise-grade. My lesson from that is that if you feel about something, it is strategic. You need to not only solve problems, but be super proactive. And also, again, this contradicts the fact of, what are the goals, what are we going to achieve because you need to lean on something which is strategic. With everything that we said at the beginning of the conversation, there is also things that you need to do because this is the company you want to build, this is the product that you want to build. And you don't necessarily get the [inaudible 01:15:23] of getting conviction from things that happened in the past or from data. You need to just go with your intuition and take this risk. And I'm super happy that we did it, but this is an example where things really broke and what we did with it.
turns.zh: 系统。他来找我，我记得突然看到门票飙升，这太难了，对吧？你说，哇，这真是太难了。你不一定有立即修复它的魔杖。我们所做的，实际上再次将每个人都连接到了它。他们做的第一件事就是向团队中的每个人展示飞盘高尔夫，并向团队中的每个人展示和思考我们可以做什么。我们做了很多事情，我们非常努力，我们设法让这种情况变得更好。然后时间过去了，你还在继续，然后又发生了。我可以在第三次说时分享这一点：“好吧，我们受够了。我们需要以不同的方式思考完全不同的问题。”过去，我认为这就是我们许多核心长期项目诞生的地方。签名是 MondayDB。这是我们在过去三年左右构建的底层数据基础设施的名称。 (01:13:19)：想想一个非常小的团队和一个非常小的初创公司。我记得那天我们说，听着，我们需要的最有才华的人现在不会再贡献功能了。我们把它们放在一个单独的地方，让我们一边思考100X一边思考并解决这个问题。在很多方面，它确实与我们在许多其他示例中讨论的内容非常不同，对吗？我想现在我们说，听着，我们希望这成为我们的竞争优势，而不是解决问题。我们拥有非常独特的产品架构，每个人都可以构建自己的表架构。就其背后的技术而言，这是一件疯狂的事情。我们想做的事情不仅能解决问题，还能为我们带来竞争优势。我们冒了巨大的风险，因为我们把很多人放在一边，或者不是很多人，而是非常有才华的人。 (01:14:27)：我认为回想起来，我们发布 MondayDB 的方式，我认为一年半前，第一个版本，它为客户带来了巨大的变化。从很多方面来说，这实际上使我们今天成为了企业级平台。我从中得到的教训是，如果你对某件事有感觉，那么它就是战略性的。你不仅需要解决问题，还需要超级积极主动。而且，这又与我们的目标是什么、我们要实现什么目标相矛盾，因为你需要依靠战略性的东西。就我们在​​谈话开始时所说的一切而言，还有一些你需要做的事情，因为这是你想要建立的公司，这是你想要建立的产品。而且你不一定能从过去发生的事情或数据中获得信念[听不清 01:15:23]。你需要跟随你的直觉并承担这个风险。我非常高兴我们做到了，但这是一个事情真正崩溃的例子以及我们用它做了什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple other stories of crisis I'm thinking back to, and they all seem to be a database started reaching capacity and we are about to fall apart 'cause their growth was too fast. That's an interesting lesson for people to hear, just try to anticipate this a little more. And sounds like that's what you realized is let's think a 100X from now, not just a couple years from now. It reminds me of, so Brian Johnson, he's this dude that's trying to live forever or as long as he can and he makes this really interesting point that I promise connects to what you're talking about, which is he's like, okay, what is your goal? He asked everyone, what's your life goal? And so they're like, oh, I want to do this and this and that. To accomplish that, the base goal you're not even thinking about is you need to not die. And that's actually the number one goal everyone should have, don't die. And I feel like that's infrastructure in companies is you have all these metrics and goals, but really the goal underneath that is your infrastructure needs to scale. It makes sense why this is outside of, okay, we have all these metrics and goals, this is-
turns.zh: 我回想起其他几个危机故事，它们似乎都是一个数据库开始达到容量，而我们即将崩溃，因为它们的增长太快了。对于人们来说，这是一个有趣的教训，只要尝试更多地预测这一点即可。听起来你意识到，让我们想想从现在起 100 倍，而不仅仅是几年后。这让我想起了布莱恩·约翰逊，他是一个试图永远活下去或尽可能活得长久的家伙，他提出了一个非常有趣的观点，我保证这与你正在谈论的内容有关，他说，好吧，你的目标是什么？他问大家，你们的人生目标是什么？所以他们就像，哦，我想做这个、这个、那个。为了实现这一目标，你甚至没有考虑过的基本目标是你需要不死。这实际上是每个人都应该拥有的首要目标，不要死。我觉得公司的基础设施是你拥有所有这些指标和目标，但真正的目标是你的基础设施需要扩展。这是有道理的，为什么这是在外面，好吧，我们有所有这些指标和目标，这是-

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Yeah. Not necessarily treating it as a tax or as a risk, but rather for our offering as a platform, this is actually now one of our core advantages. It's super important as well, that value to customers comes in different ways, shapes and forms. And you need to think about the experience and not only about... And many times the general experience start with things that are reliable, performant, that you can count on them and suddenly you even use them differently because they're fast. I think this is another important aspect to it.
turns.zh: 是的。不一定将其视为税收或风险，而是对于我们作为平台的产品而言，这实际上现在是我们的核心优势之一。同样非常重要的是，对客户的价值有不同的方式、形式和形式。你需要考虑体验，而不仅仅是……很多时候，一般体验都是从可靠的、高性能的、你可以信赖的东西开始的，突然间你甚至会以不同的方式使用它们，因为它们很快。我认为这是它的另一个重要方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point. When you have a problem, something that's slowing you down or might crumble the company, just not flipping it from how do we just put the bandaid here? How do we turn this into a strategic advantage if we really invest the time? I like that a lot. Okay. To start to close out our conversation, I'm going to take us to AI Corner, which is a recurring segment I try to get to more and more with this podcast. And the question is, what's an example of you using AI tools in your day-to-day work to do better work, to do faster work that you think might be helpful to other folks?
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。当你遇到问题时，有些事情会拖慢你的速度，或者可能会导致公司崩溃，但如果你不把它从我们如何把创可贴放在这里的地方翻转过来呢？如果我们真的投入时间，如何将其转化为战略优势？我非常喜欢这样。好的。为了结束我们的谈话，我将带我们去人工智能角，这是我试图通过这个播客越来越多地了解的一个反复出现的部分。问题是，您在日常工作中使用人工智能工具来更好、更快地完成您认为可能对其他人有帮助的工作的例子是什么？

turns.speaker: Daniel Lereya
turns.en: Maybe I start with a personal one. It's not about work, but I think it really shows that for me, it was a moment of really saying this has so much potential in it. I actually prepared myself for a marathon and unfortunately I got injured in my knee. Yeah/ I went to do an MRI scan and I finished the scan and they gave me this disc with the results and then they said, "Listen, you need to schedule a doctor appointment five days from now." Okay. I said, I took it, put it in ChatGPT and ask for the results, an explanation of line by line, what does it mean. And then I of course went to the doctor and said, these are the results. But I think for me, this is something that I was really happy about using it and it also opens my mind a lot because I think that if you think about it from the product perspective, and this is how we think about AI in Monday, the technology is amazing, you can do so much with it, but there's still the part of productizing it because every person that I talked with him about this example, with enthusiasm he said, "How did you think about putting your MRI there?" (01:19:15): And I said, "I don't know, I just did." But this is all creating products that actually allow people to leverage this technology. And more on the work side, I use it a lot. I think for me, one recent example I would say is we really worked hard towards determining the pricing for AI offering that I was mentioning earlier. And just in two hours I managed to get the full perspective on what everyone else are doing. And we have analysts and we have product managers, but the fact that I was independent and managed to get the initial thoughts and all the information in just a bit, it was mind-blowing. I use it a lot in order to understand things that are very extensive, what the competitors are doing, what is the history of this and that. And I think it helped me a lot in that sense.
